small_guidance:
- The GEMM is M=128, N=16384, K=16384 — M is tiny so BLOCK_M=32 or 64 with BLOCK_N=128/256 is correct, but add configs with BLOCK_K=128 and num_stages=3-4 to better hide K-loop loads; also try `num_warps=8` with `BLOCK_M=32, BLOCK_N=128, BLOCK_K=128`.
- The softmax kernel uses 3 passes reading global memory each time. Since N=16384 fits, use a single-pass online softmax or at minimum cache the loaded tile in registers across passes by tiling with BLOCK_N=16384 (one block covers the row); set `num_warps=16` or use `tl.max`/`tl.sum` over the full row in one shot.
- Fuse dropout (inference mode dropout is identity since `model.eval()` is typical, but here it runs in training mode by default — verify; if eval, drop the dropout call entirely; if train, fuse the Bernoulli mask + scale into the softmax-input load to save a full pass over a 128×16384 tensor).
large_guidance:
- Fuse the bias-add + dropout + softmax into the GEMM epilogue as a persistent row-parallel kernel: one program per output row computes its full 16384-wide row by streaming K in tiles, accumulating into row registers, then performing online softmax (max + sum + normalize) and writing once. With M=128, launching 128 programs (or 128×row-split) keeps the SMs busy and eliminates two extra global passes.
- Alternatively, split the work into two kernels but redesign the softmax as a single-pass online algorithm (Welford-style running max + renormalized sum) so the input tensor is read once instead of three times — at N=16384 fp32 per row, that's a 3× memory-traffic win on the softmax stage.
- Consider using tensor cores via fp16/bf16 for the GEMM (cast weight once at init, accumulate in fp32) — K=16384 with fp32 `tl.dot` is leaving most of the 4090's throughput on the table.
